title: Climate Change Data and Models
seo_title: Climate Change Worksheets: Warming Rates, Sea Level, Sea Ice and Climate Models (Earth Science)
standard_text: Analyze geoscience data and the results from global climate models to make an evidence-based forecast of the current rate of global or regional climate change and associated future impacts to Earth systems.
meta_desc: Free high school Earth and space science worksheets on climate change data and models (NGSS HS-ESS3-5): warming rates, forecasts, sea-level rise, Arctic sea ice, evidence of impacts and emissions scenarios. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Temperature, ice and sea-level data show the trend; models give a range.
body_html:
How to think about it

Use data to find the rate, then forecast with a range.

  • Rate of change = (later value − earlier value) ÷ time. Climate rates are often given per decade.
  • Forecast: today's value + rate × time. Models give ranges because future emissions are uncertain.
  • Evidence: rising temperatures, shrinking glaciers and Arctic sea ice, rising seas, earlier springs, coral bleaching.
Example

+0.2 °C in 1980, +0.8 °C in 2010. Rate?

0.6 ÷ 3 decades

Answer: 0.2 °C per decade

Example

Sea level rises 4 mm/year. Rise in 50 years?

4 × 50 = 200 mm

Answer: 20 cm

Common mistakes

  • Using one cold winter to judge the climate.
  • Using the last value as the rate.
  • Thinking models give one exact number.

faq.q: How do you find the rate of climate change from data?
faq.a: Subtract the earlier value from the later value and divide by the time between them. For temperature, the rate is often given in °C per decade.

faq.q: Why do climate forecasts give a range?
faq.a: Future emissions depend on human choices, and some processes such as clouds and ice-sheet melting are not known exactly.

faq.q: What evidence shows the climate is changing?
faq.a: Rising global temperatures, shrinking glaciers and Arctic sea ice, rising sea level, earlier springs and more frequent heat waves all point to warming.
